summary: SAR Alibi changes NISAR change detections into verifiable investigations of competing physical explanations. Instead of labelling every radar anomaly "flood" it segments changed regions, and tests open water, flooded vegetation, soil wetting, vegetation or harvest change, deformation, and processing artefacts against HH/GV responses, rainfall, event context, and geometry controls. Every region shows signed support, counter evidence, missing tests, evidence coverage, and a next observation that could discriminate among surviving explanations. Where the evidence is weak, SAR Alibi reports "unresolved" rather than showing certainty. Our working mozambique prototype compares two matched NISAR acquisitions from 5 jan and 17 jan 2026, contextualised by NASA POWER rainfall and NASA's published flood visualisations. It includes an interactive map, clickable evidence ledgers, negative controls, reference comparisons, and reproducible exports. The public demonstrator labels its calculations as dispay derived, a separate calibrated GCOV pipeline is included for authenticated quantitative analysis. SAR Alibi helps analysts move from "something changed" to a defensible inspectable next step.
details:
SAR Alibi addresses the gap between detecting surface change and explaining its physical driver. An increase or decrease in is not an unique flood signature. Wet soil, vegetation conditions, inundated vegetation, acquisition geometry, and processing differences can produce ambiguous observations. SAR Alibi preserves the ambiguity and makes reasoning inspectable.

The web app matches repeat NISAR scenes, calculates HH/HV log ratio change, filters and segments candidates, and calculates reliable regional measurements. A deterministic evidence engine compares six rival explanations: open-water flood, flooded vegetation, soil wetting, vegetation/harvest change, deformation, and geometry artefacts.

Each hypothesis has explicit predicted observations, signed compatibility, reliability, design weights, and counter tests. Compatibility and evidence coverage are reported separately, preventing a region from appearing well supported merely because necessary observations are absent. Missing evidence remains neutral rather than being treated as an observed contradiction. Deformation remains visibly untestable without suitable GUNW displacement or coherence evidence.

The user can swipe between pre-event and post-event imagery, enable change and candidate overlays, zoom and pan, select regions, inspect measurements and individual evidence tests, search and filter regions, run ablations, and expect region JSON or filtered geo JSON too. Showcase buttons open a resolved case, an unresolved case, and an artefact review case. The next-observation panel recommends evidence such as cloud-free optical imagery, an independent water record, or same geometry quantitative GCOV review.

The current public run identifies 129 candidate regions, 67 resolved, 61 unresolved and 1 artefact review. The abstention is intentional, R8-01 leads with open-water flood; R-068 remains unresolved with soil wetting narrowly ahead; R-003 enters artefact review because its very low pre-event return occurs near the scene edge, The NASA SVS reference threshold sweep reports its best same-reference-tuned result as F1 0.4436, precision 0.3959, recall 0.5044, and IoU 0.285. This isn't independent accuracy validation: the reference is a published visualisation from the same mission and event, and the threshold was tuned on it. 3 analyst-selected low change controls, simple detection and flood-only baselines, and eight acquisition mismatch sends all 129 regions to artefact review. The deliberately invalid missing-as-zero variant inflated mean coverage to 1.0 without creating new evidence. 24 scientific tests passed.

The prototype compares NISAR L2 GCOV BETA scenes from 5 jan and 17 jan 2026, track 114, frame 165 ascending, DHDH, on a 12-day repeat. Exact CMR records are: G4058657013-ASF and G4059040862-ASF. NASA POWER supplies daily rainfall context near Chókwè, and NASA SVS 5661 supplies published event visualisations. The public demonstrator uses official 8-bit ASF NISAR quicklooks and computes genuine change rasters from their display channels. It does not describe those values as calibrated γ⁰ or operational flood science. Both scenes use the same BETA processing lineage. Each quicklook is approximately georeferenced using its own CMR polygon. Exact pair metadata, formulas, hashes, limitations, and downloads are available in the Provenance view. A seperate quantitative route is included for the original L2 GCOV HDF5 granules. It verifies native grids and processing lineage, reads HHHH/HVHV linear γ⁰ power, applies join validity checks, and computes γ⁰ based dB log ratios. This route has synthetic HDF5 integration tests. Real HDF5 processing was not completed in the credential free build environment, so no completed calibrated result is there.

SAR Alibi combines region-level NISAR change segmentation, competing physical driver signature tests, signed counter evidence, acquisition controls, separate evidence coverage, abstention, and next evidence recommendations in one reproducible workflow. Prior art exists in change-cause estimation, multisource flood fusion, observation ranking, operational quality layers, and abstention. This project is designed for analysts, students and response researchers who need to determine what can responsibly be concluded after a change detection. Its immediate value is reducing unsupported single cause interpretation and revealing missing or contradictory evidence.

The analysis uses Python, Numpy, Scipy, OpenCV, Pillow, Rasterio, Shapely, h5py, pyproj, Affine, earthaccess, requests, and pytest. The interface uses React, Typescript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, Lucide icons, and custom SVG geospatial rendering. All map and analysis assets are local, no backend, account system, or API key is needed. No language model assigns a region verdict either.
